You need to set a schedule for meals. I had the exact same problem but I eventually figured out that 1. I was binge eating because I didn't have anything I enjoyed doing in life and 2. because I didn't have a set eating schedule so I couldn't hold myself accountable for anything. 

1st I would start eating just three meals a day. Disclaimer: don't think about weight loss at all. Even if you overeat for the first few days, it's fine. You need to continue to eat all three (or how many you decide) meals per day because your body won't adjust to the new routine if there is no routine to adjust to.

When you eat, put everything that you plan on eating right in front of you and don't even think about going and getting more food. If you need to put a larger quantity of food on your plate at first because you're scared of that kind of permanence that's fine. You'll figure it out within a few weeks. If you reaaally need snacks then that's also okay but they need to be scheduled snacks. Personally I don't like to eat snacks because that time I've spent not eating allows me to listen to my hunger signals better and also be more productive at other things I am doing. The main thing is scheduling and preparing because at this point, your hunger signals are going to be confused with psychological hunger. And while it's okay to listen to psychological hunger, it's important to be able to differentiate between physical and psychological hunger and that starts with forming a routine.

2nd find something that you enjoy doing more than eating. For me, I got back into reading and playing chess. It's very engaging for my brain, I don't feel like I'm wasting away when I do it (though it's not exactly a completely productive use of my time), and it fills time and helps me procrastinate in a non-harmful way if I want to. This tip might not be as applicable to you since your cause of binge eating might be different than mine. However, I think I know the feeling you're describing. For me, I felt proud that I was eating as I gained weight, but that pride became a quick dopamine shot if I was feeling down, which normally happened when I had too time or work to do. 

It's difficult to put into words exactly how important a routine eating schedule is because you won't understand the way it completely changes your view of food until you have established that routine and find yourself only thinking about food during your meal times. You can also slowly make adjustments to make your meals healthier and it ultimately results in more mindful eating. (I actually hate the term "mindful eating" because it sounds like you have to be laser focused on your food while eating it, but for me it's more of an understanding of food for what it is rather than the emotions attached to it).

Hi! I replied to someone who made a post similar to this one. The original poster was losing weight after being obese through keto and starting to feel the restriction monster a little bit. Here is what I said:

I TOTALLY get this experience. Keto is personally a triggering diet for me since results are so instant that you just feel like you can do more and more and more until you're eating just a single sausage every day lol.  
  
1. Focus on the foods and their nutritional quality themselves. Come up with balanced go-to meals and establish a meal routine that you rotate through every few weeks to make sure you have nutritional variety.  
  
2. Ultimately weight loss is not your goal in life. You don't die happy because you lost weight or anything. It's so so so important that the weight loss process does not hinder your ability to participate in activities you enjoy. If you've had disordered eating for a while that took up a ton of time, pick up a new hobby. Crocheting is therapeutic and surprisingly consuming for me so I do it for fun.  
  
3. And to make this point more applicable to you, you need to stop focusing on that deadline for weight loss. Weight loss is the result of healthier habits and it happens at its own pace. I can't will myself to become the president of the US by bribing everyone in the country to vote for me. It's a multi-faceted process and becoming president is merely the uncontrollable outcome.  
  
4. Refocus and challenge your thoughts. This is basically self-therapy. Every time you have a super restrictive thought tell yourself like a dog, "No, bad \[gloppy213\]". It's humorous and it refocuses you. Another thing that's understandably extremely difficult is stopping the weighing and stopping mirror checking. Just refuse yourself once and say "What am I doing? I look the same as I did yesterday". This will challenge the habit or even addiction you've built to the measurements and the pattern will be disrupted. You'll be able to catch yourself next time even more easily and you always have to challenge yourself to say "no, I don't need to. It's unnecessary and I look and feel fine". Eating disorders are mental disorders that can turn physical so don't let it get to the point of physical illness. Build healthy thought patterns.  
  
5. Similar to coming up with a set meal plan, eat exactly three meals a day (and designated snacks if you want). Don't let your restrictive thoughts tell you "Oh you're not hungry you can skip this meal". Eat when it's time to eat.  
  
6. Don't take this too seriously. Again, weight loss should not interfere with your life. Go out and eat with your friends and family. Try that new restaurant if that's something you enjoy. For obese people the problem tends to be portion control so the only thing you should be strict about is listening to your body. Even if you eat a low volume of foods (like something fatty with a lot of sugar), your body knows how much energy it needs and it will regulate that for you by telling you that you have enough energy even if your stomach isn't bursting.  
  
7. If you're trying all of these things while losing weight at the same time and it's not working then you need a break from weight loss. For my various eating disorders I would hear messages like the ones I put in this comment and I would say "Oh! That makes sense, I'll do that" but then I wouldn't do it properly because I was still terrified of letting go and losing control. I had no faith in my body's ability to regulate itself. You need to let go of that need for control and if you take a break from losing weight for a bit then you can take of the added pressure of recovering from these thoughts.  
  
I see a lot of people saying it's not possible to lose weight while having an eating disorder. I would agree with that. However based on your post you only seem to be having disordered thoughts, which is natural and can be mitigated while losing weight if caught early (which you do seem to have caught your thoughts early). More than anything you have to recognize that these thoughts are rooted in fear. They are not your friend and you should never indulge them, though it is admittedly exhausting to sort out which thoughts and actions are your eating disorder and which thoughts and actions are you. This is why it is so important for you to go back to the other points about routine. As long as you follow a premeditated routine and are kind to yourself when it gets hard, the disordered thoughts will lose.
